<document>
# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
I've read it and checked it against the four earlier documents.

## What it reports

**Varden case-processing offices, 24 months, with randomisation maintained.**
- **Output per employee:** −3.4% (CI −8.0 to +1.2).
- **Hours:** timesheet hours fell 12%. A new measure, active log-in time on the case-management system, fell 11%.
- **Output per hour:** +9.8% on timesheets and +8.5% on system logs, down from +12.5% at nine months.
- **Mediation:** a mediation test, registered at month 11, attributes 47% of the per-hour gain to fewer recurring meetings, 18% to lower fatigue, and leaves 35% unexplained.
- **Quality, sickness and retention:** quality is unchanged, sick days are down 27%, and resignations remain about half of control.

**Varden counter offices.** The county ended this arm at month 12. Waits were 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control, and restoring service would have needed about 12% more staff.

**An unplanned observation.** Two control offices cut meetings on their own initiative and gained 4.1% in output per hour over their own previous six months.

**Halden subset.** Of 23 organisations with output records, 14 responded and 3 of those had reverted. The 11 that continued show +11.8% output per actual hour. The authors label this an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours.

**Response to earlier claims.** The "entirely an artifact" claim fails under the critique's own recommended standards. The meta-analysis's four long-follow-up studies were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, so they cannot say anything about decay.

## Arithmetic

The headline figures check out:
- 0.966/0.88 gives +9.8%, and 0.966/0.89 gives +8.5%.
- 96.8/0.866 gives +11.8%.
- The meetings difference-in-differences (−3.5 treated against −0.2 control) matches the 3.3-hour gap at month six.
- The mediation shares sum to 100%.

The counter staffing figure (12%) is close to the 1/0.886 ≈ 13% implied by the nine-month results.

## What this settles

These three findings should now carry their full weight:

1. **There is a per-hour gain, and it lasts at least two years in this setting.** The estimate is +8.5% (3.4 to 13.8), using records, log-measured hours, randomisation and a 24-month horizon. "Entirely an artifact" is refuted here. My earlier summary called durability "open". For discretionary public-sector case-processing over 24 months, it is now answered.
2. **The meetings pathway is real and substantial.** It survived a registered test, and the comment's dismissal of it as post hoc doesn't hold. The comment was right that a correlation across seven offices couldn't establish a mechanism. It was wrong to conclude the mechanism wasn't there.
3. **Coverage-bound work can't absorb the cut without more staff.** The county ended the counter arm because of service levels, and costed the fix.

## Issues

**1. The Summary compares two different measures.**
"Fell from 12.5% to 8.5%" sets the nine-month timesheet figure against the 24-month log figure. The like-for-like comparison is 12.5% to 9.8%. The body handles this correctly, but the Summary overstates the decline.

**2. The decline isn't tested, and it may be partly contamination.**
The intervals for the two timesheet estimates (6.9–18.4 and 4.6–15.2) overlap heavily. The paper doesn't report a test of the difference, so "the gain has declined" is a point-estimate statement, not an established result. Section 5's "declined by about a quarter" asserts more than the data show. In that respect it mirrors the meta-analysis, which concluded too firmly in the other direction.

There is also a concrete alternative explanation the paper doesn't draw out. Two of the seven control offices adopted the mechanism itself at month 15 and improved by 4.1%. That raises control output and shrinks the treated-minus-control difference.

As a rough estimate: 2/7 × 4.1% ≈ 1.2 points. That could account for close to half of the 2.7-point fall (12.5 to 9.8), depending on which months the 24-month estimate covers. Re-estimating with those two offices excluded, or with month-15 contamination modelled, would show how much of the decline is genuine fading.

A related check: if those two offices cut meetings from 7.1 to 5.0 hours, the control average should fall by about 0.6 hours. The reported fall is 0.2 (7.2 to 7.0). Either other control offices increased their meetings, or the figures cover different periods. One sentence would reconcile this.

**3. What do the system logs measure, and does it conflict with the meetings data?**
This is the most substantive question. The logs are described as recording "time staff are working on cases." If that excludes meetings, the meetings data imply that case-work time fell much less than 11%.

The rough accounting uses the nine-month baseline of about 37.9 hours and assumes control hours were stable:

| | Timesheet hours | Meetings | Non-meeting hours |
|---|---|---|---|
| Treated | 37.9 × 0.88 ≈ 33.4 | 3.9 | ≈ 29.5 |
| Control | ≈ 37.9 | 7.0 | ≈ 30.9 |

Non-meeting time falls about 5%, not 11%, and output per non-meeting hour rises only about 1–2%. This repeats the nine-month estimate of about 3% from my earlier note.

That leaves two possibilities:
- **The logs include meeting time** (staff stay logged in during meetings). Then "active time on cases" is the wrong description. The 47% mediation share is then partly mechanical, because removing low-output hours from the denominator raises output per hour by definition. Economically that is still a real gain to the employer. But it is a gain from removing unproductive time, not from working faster.
- **The logs exclude meetings.** Then the 11% figure and the meetings figures are hard to reconcile.

Either way, a simple accounting attributes more than 47% of the gain to meetings, possibly most of it. The paper should define the log measure precisely and say why the mediation estimate and the accounting differ.

**4. Mediation precision with 14 clusters.**
"A larger sample of office-months" adds observations but not independent units, since the effective sample is still 14 offices. An interval of 28–66% looks narrow for 14 clusters. The paper should state how clustering was handled, for example with a cluster bootstrap. The confounding assumption in the limitations is the right caveat, and it deserves more weight than one sentence.

**5. The marketing agency doesn't fit "coverage".**
"All with client-facing or coverage obligations" groups a marketing agency citing client deadlines with retail and hospitality citing opening hours. Under the meta-analysis's coding, marketing is discretionary work. This may point to a third category: work driven by client responsiveness, which is neither freely schedulable nor tied to physical presence. That would be a useful refinement, rather than something to fold into "coverage."

**6. Smaller points.**
- **Halden baseline hours.** The 40.3-hour baseline is the comment's 27-organisation figure. The 11 continuing organisations should use their own baseline (the comment's 17-organisation subset averaged 40.4).
- **Non-response.** Nine of the 23 Halden organisations didn't respond. They should be noted alongside the "survivors twice over" caveat, as a third filter.
- **Co-authorship.** R. Okafor co-wrote the original Halden paper. This doesn't change the analysis, which is candid about the Halden subset's limits, but it is worth a disclosure line.

## Where things now stand

**Settled for discretionary public-sector case-processing over 24 months:**
- Output per actual hour rises by about 8–10%.
- Output per employee falls slightly, by about 3%, with a lower bound near −8%.
- Quality holds, and sickness and resignations fall.
- A large share of the gain comes from cutting meetings.

**Settled for coverage-bound work:**
- Service falls unless staff are added. Here that meant roughly 12% more staff and a 9% rise in cost per contact.

**Still open:**
- **The size of any decay.** It may be partly contamination (issue 2).
- **The exact share due to meetings.** The mediation estimate and the accounting differ (issue 3).
- **Whether the gain is available without cutting hours.** This is the question the paper rightly identifies as unanswerable from this trial.

That last question is now the most consequential. It decides whether the policy is "cut hours" or "cut meetings." The design that answers it is a three-arm trial: hours reduction, a meeting audit at unchanged hours, and control. The two control offices that audited on their own show it can be implemented in this setting.

I can sketch that three-arm design, including power at 7 offices per arm. I can also draft a short note to the authors on issues 2 and 3, which are the ones most likely to change the headline numbers.
